Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Dahr is Medinan and has thirty-one verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, which We test; and We made him hearing and seeing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor,﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly.﴾ ﴿They fulfil their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾ ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive.﴾ ﴿"We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not desire from you reward or thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is frowning and distressing."﴾ ﴿So Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and will give them radiance and joy.﴾ ﴿And He will reward them, for what they endured, with a garden and silk.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein on couches, they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold.﴾ ﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in submission.﴾.

This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Mujahid and Qatadah said it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said it is Medinan except for one verse, which is Meccan, namely: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. It was also said that it is Medinan except for His words: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 24] and so on, for this is Meccan; this was related by al-Mawardi. Its connection to what precedes it is very clear and needs no explanation.

(Hal) is an interrogative particle. If it enters upon a nominal sentence, it cannot be interpreted as qad (indeed, already), because qad is one of the distinguishing features of the verb. If it enters upon a verb, it most commonly comes for pure interrogation. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said that here it has the meaning of qad. It was said: this is because the original form was (ahal), so the hamzah was dropped and the particle alone was used for interrogation. This is shown by the verse:

*"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about their encampment: did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, which has hills?"*

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come upon man, a short time ago, a period of time, approximately and generally, in which he was not such-and-such?" The answer then is: "It came upon him while he was in the state mentioned." It was recited in the presence of Abu Bakr, or it was said in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "I wish it had been completed," meaning: I wish that state had been completed, namely that he was a thing not worth mentioning, not yet created and not yet obligated.

Here "man" (al-insan) refers to the whole species of the children of Adam. The period of time that passed over him was either the time of his non-existence or the time of his being a drop of sperm. His movement from one stage to another, until the time when he could be addressed, is a period in which he had no mention; he is called "man" by reference to what he became. It was also said: the one meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and the period that passed over him is the duration in which he remained until the spirit was breathed into him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he remained as clay for forty years, then as dried clay for forty years, then as black mud moulded for forty years, so his creation was completed in one hundred and twenty years, and he is called "man" by reference to what he came to be.

The clause "he was not" (lam yakun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "man," as if it were said: "not worth mentioning." This is the apparent meaning. Or it is in the position of an attributive clause (sifa) for "a period" (hin), in which case the returning pronoun referring to the modified noun is omitted, meaning: "he was not in it."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: he is the species of the children of Adam, because Adam was not created from a sperm-drop. ﴿A mixture﴾: that is, a combination of ingredients, and it is an attribute of the sperm-drop. Ibn Mas'ud and Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father, said: they are the veins that are in the sperm-drop. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it is the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, which mixed in the womb, and man was created from both of them. Al-Hasan said: it is the mixing of the sperm-drop with menstrual blood, for when a woman conceives, menstruation stops. Ibn 'Abbas also, along with 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, said: they are mixtures moving from a sperm-drop to a clot, to a lump of flesh, and to other stages, until man is brought into being. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with al-Kalbi, said: they are the colours of the sperm-drop. It was said: they are mixtures of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The sperm-drop is intended as a species, which is why it is described with a plural, like His words: ﴿on green cushions﴾ [al-Rahman: 76]; or because each part of the sperm-drop is treated as a sperm-drop.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "sperm-drop mixture" (nutfatin amshaj) is like "a cooking pot of firewood" (burmatin a'sar) and "a garment of fibres" (burdin akyas), and these are singular nouns which are not plurals, which is why they occur as attributes of singulars. It is also said: "a sperm-drop of mashaj" (nutfatu mashajin), and amshaj cannot be a broken plural of it; rather, both are equal in being singular, since a singular is described by them. End of quote. His statement contradicts the explicit text of Sibawayh and the grammarians that af'al (the pattern of amshaj) does not occur as a singular. Sibawayh said: "There is no af'al in speech except that it is broken from a noun which functions as a collective; and whatever is reported of a singular being described by af'al, they have interpreted it."

﴿We test him﴾: We examine him through legal obligation in this world. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: We turn him about in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop and then a clot. According to this view, the clause is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (hal musahiba). According to the view that the meaning is testing him by obligation, it is a future circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because when He created him from a sperm-drop, He was not yet testing him with obligation at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also mean that We move him from one state to another, and that testing has been called such by way of metaphor. End of quote. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement. It was also said: We test him with the creation and existence in this world, so it is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech; the original order is: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾, while "We test him" follows; that is, making him hearing and seeing is the testing. There is no need to claim inversion, and the meaning is sound without it. He bestowed upon him a favour by making him with these two attributes, and they are an allusion to discernment and understanding, since their instruments are the cause of that; and they are the noblest of the senses, by which the greatest things are perceived.

When He had made him in this condition, He informed that He guided him to the way, that is: He directed him to the path and made known to him the outcome of the path of salvation and the outcome of the path of destruction, since He directed him to the path of guidance. Mujahid said: the way of happiness and misery. Al-Suddi said: the way out of the womb. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We enabled him and empowered him in both his states; and when We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, it was known from Him that he would either believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof. End of quote, and this is according to the method of entailment (iltizam).

The majority read (imma) with a kasra on the hamzah in both places. Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-'Aj, who is Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sulami, a Syrian who was governor of Basra for Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, read it with a fatha in both places. This is a dialect related by Abu Zayd from the Arabs, and it is the one that some people counted among the conjunctions (huruf al-'atf). They recited:

*"There will overtake her either a harsh north wind, or the blowing of an east wind at the end of the evening."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a good reading, and the meaning is: either grateful, by Our guidance, or ungrateful, through his own bad choice. End of quote. He made "إمّا" (imma) the detailed (tafsili) particle that carries the sense of a condition, which is why it is followed by the particle of response (fa'), so it becomes like the Arabs' saying: "Imma sadiqan fa-sadiqun" (either a friend, then a friend). "Shakiran" and "kafuran" are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the pronoun of object in ﴿هَدَيْناهُ﴾ (We guided him). Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that they be two states of "al-sabil" (the way), meaning: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ (And We guided him to the two highways) [al-Balad: 10], where He described the way with gratitude and disbelief figuratively. End of quote. Since few people are characterised by gratitude, He said "shakiran" (grateful). Since disbelief is common, and many people are characterised by it, and its occurrence from man is frequent, unlike gratitude, He came with "kafuran" in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). When He mentioned the two groups, He followed them with the threat and the promise.

Talha, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ (salasila) without tanwin (diptote) both in pause and in continuation. It is reported from Hamza and Abu 'Amr that in pause they used the alif. Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan read it without tanwin, and there is difference of transmission from them regarding pause, and likewise from al-Bazzi. The remaining seven read it with tanwin in continuation, and with the alif replacing it in pause; this is the reading of al-A'mash. It is said: This is according to what al-Akhfash related of the dialect of those who give tanwin to every word that is not declined except "af'al min", and this is the dialect of the poets, then it became common until it became part of their speech. He explained this by saying that this plural, since it is pluralised (again), as they said: "sawahibat Yusuf" and "nawakisi al-absar," resembled the singular, so tanwin was applied to it. One of the rajaz poets said:

"Tanwin in the plural has come frequently, until a people claimed with it the option."

The tanwin is established in the mushafs of Madina, Makka, Kufa and Basra, and in the mushafs of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah; likewise "qawarir." Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: "salasila" in continuation, and "salasila" with an alif without tanwin in pause. It is also reported that among the Arabs there are those who say: "ra'aytu 'Amra" with the alif in pause.

﴿مِن كَأْسٍ﴾ (from a cup): "min" indicates the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). ﴿كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾ (its mixture is camphor). Qatada said: It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It is also said that this is by way of comparison, meaning: fragrant of smell and coolness like camphor. Al-Kalbi said: "Kafuran" is the name of a spring in Paradise, and it was given tanwin to match the verse-endings. 'Abd Allah read "qafuran" with qaf in place of kaf; these two often interchange within a word, as in the saying: "'arabi quhhun" and "kuhhun" (pure Arab).

"'Aynan" is a substitute for "kafuran" and an object of ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ﴾ (they drink), meaning: water of a spring; or it is a substitute from the position of "min ka's" with an elided noun, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring; or it is put in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas). Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. He used the "ba'" which indicates joining (al-ilsaq), and the meaning: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, as you say: "I drank water with honey." Or "yashrabu" is taken to imply "yarwa" (to quench), and so it takes "ba'". It is also said: the "ba'" is extra and the meaning is "yashrabu biha"; al-Hudhali said:

"They drank the water of the sea, then they rose, and to them, in the upper reaches of green seas, is a groaning."

It was said: that is, they drank the water of the sea. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yashraba-ha."

﴿عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾ (the servants of Allah) here are the believers. ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها﴾ (they cause it to gush): they pierce it with a cane stalk or the like wherever they wish, so it flows for each one of them; this is how it is reported in the narration. It is also said: it is a spring in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that gushes out to the houses of the prophets and the believers.

﴿يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ﴾ (they fulfil the vow) in this world, and they used to fear. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿يُوفُونَ﴾ is the answer to one who might say: "Why are they given that?" End of quote. Thus he used "'asa" as a relative for "man," which is not permissible, and after "'asa" he used the present tense not preceded by "an," which is rare or found only in poetry. The apparent meaning is that "nadhr" refers to what is well known in the Sharia as a vow. Al-Asamm, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being diligent in performing obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself will be more faithful to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon him. It is also said: the "nadhr" here is general, covering what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory and what the servant has made obligatory upon himself, so faith and all acts of obedience are included in it.

﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. The first is more praiseworthy, because it involves preferring others over oneself; as for the second, the wealthy may do it more often. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is a captive from the people of the qibla. It is said: "wa-asiran" is a metaphor and a figure of speech. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is the imprisoned person. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."

﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾ (We feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance): this is by implying a saying (idmar al-qawl). It is permissible that they declared it explicitly, addressing those mentioned, to prevent them from reciprocating with the like or with thanks, since their kindness is done for the countenance of Allah the Exalted, so there is no sense in repaying the creation; and this is the apparent meaning. Mujahid said: As for them, they did not speak it, but Allah the Exalted knew it from them, so He praised them for it.

﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. This verse was said to have been revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face. Al-Naqqash mentioned in this a very long narrative, apparently full of disagreement; in it there is an indication for the needy, the orphan and the captive, who are addressed with it in the house of prophethood, and an indication for Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, who addresses each of them; its outward form is disagreement, due to the baseness of its wording, the breaking of its verses and the triviality of its meanings.

﴿يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا﴾ (a stern day): attributing sternness to the day is a metaphor. Ibn 'Abbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from his eyes like tar. The majority read ﴿فَوَقاهُمُ﴾ (so Allah will protect them) with a light qaf; Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled.

﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." It is also said: they will not see in it a sun or a moon, and "al-zamharir" in the dialect of Tayy is the moon.

The majority read ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ (and near). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) coordinated with ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ (reclining). He also said: it is permissible that it be an attribute of the garden, so the meaning is: and He recompensed them with a near garden. Al-Zamakhshari said, in meaning, that it is a circumstantial state coordinated upon another state, which is "la yarawna" (they will not see), that is, not seeing; the waw entered to indicate that both matters are combined for them, as if it were said: and He recompensed them with a garden in which they combine between distance from heat and cold and the nearness of the shades over them. Abu Haywa read "wa-daniyatun" with raf', and al-Akhfash used it as evidence for the permissibility of raising the active participle without its being preceded by a dependent, such as your saying: "qa'imun al-zaydun" (standing are the Zaydun); but there is no proof in it, because the more apparent reading is that ﴿ظِلالُها﴾ (its shades) is the subject and ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ is its predicate. Al-A'mash read "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," which is like His saying: ﴿خاشِعَةً أبْصارُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes humbled) [al-Ma'arij: 44]. Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "sperm-drop mixture" (nutfatin amshaj) is like "a cooking pot of firewood" (burmatin a'sar) and "a garment of fibres" (burdin akyas), and these are singular nouns which are not plurals, which is why they occur as attributes of singulars. It is also said: "a sperm-drop of mashaj" (nutfatu mashajin), and amshaj cannot be a broken plural of it; rather, both are equal in being singular, since a singular is described by them. End of quote. His statement contradicts the explicit text of Sibawayh and the grammarians that af'al (the pattern of amshaj) does not occur as a singular. Sibawayh said: "There is no af'al in speech except that it is broken from a noun which functions as a collective; and whatever is reported of a singular being described by af'al, they have interpreted it."

﴿We test him﴾: We examine him through legal obligation in this world. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: We turn him about in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop and then a clot. According to this view, the clause is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (hal musahiba). According to the view that the meaning is testing him by obligation, it is a future circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because when He created him from a sperm-drop, He was not yet testing him with obligation at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also mean that We move him from one state to another, and that testing has been called such by way of metaphor. End of quote. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement. It was also said: We test him with the creation and existence in this world, so it is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech; the original order is: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾, while "We test him" follows; that is, making him hearing and seeing is the testing. There is no need to claim inversion, and the meaning is sound without it. He bestowed upon him a favour by making him with these two attributes, and they are an allusion to discernment and understanding, since their instruments are the cause of that; and they are the noblest of the senses, by which the greatest things are perceived.

When He had made him in this condition, He informed that He guided him to the way, that is: He directed him to the path and made known to him the outcome of the path of salvation and the outcome of the path of destruction, since He directed him to the path of guidance. Mujahid said: the way of happiness and misery. Al-Suddi said: the way out of the womb. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We enabled him and empowered him in both his states; and when We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, it was known from Him that he would either believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof. End of quote, and this is according to the method of entailment (iltizam).

The majority read (imma) with a kasra on the hamzah in both places. Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-'Aj, who is Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sulami, a Syrian who was governor of Basra for Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, read it with a fatha in both places. This is a dialect related by Abu Zayd from the Arabs, and it is the one that some people counted among the conjunctions (huruf al-'atf). They recited:

*"There will overtake her either a harsh north wind, or the blowing of an east wind at the end of the evening."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a good reading, and the meaning is: either grateful, by Our guidance, or ungrateful, through his own bad choice. End of quote. He made "إمّا" (imma) the detailed (tafsili) particle that carries the sense of a condition, which is why it is followed by the particle of response (fa'), so it becomes like the Arabs' saying: "Imma sadiqan fa-sadiqun" (either a friend, then a friend). "Shakiran" and "kafuran" are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the pronoun of object in ﴿هَدَيْناهُ﴾ (We guided him). Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that they be two states of "al-sabil" (the way), meaning: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ (And We guided him to the two highways) [al-Balad: 10], where He described the way with gratitude and disbelief figuratively. End of quote. Since few people are characterised by gratitude, He said "shakiran" (grateful). Since disbelief is common, and many people are characterised by it, and its occurrence from man is frequent, unlike gratitude, He came with "kafuran" in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). When He mentioned the two groups, He followed them with the threat and the promise.

Talha, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ (salasila) without tanwin (diptote) both in pause and in continuation. It is reported from Hamza and Abu 'Amr that in pause they used the alif. Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan read it without tanwin, and there is difference of transmission from them regarding pause, and likewise from al-Bazzi. The remaining seven read it with tanwin in continuation, and with the alif replacing it in pause; this is the reading of al-A'mash. It is said: This is according to what al-Akhfash related of the dialect of those who give tanwin to every word that is not declined except "af'al min", and this is the dialect of the poets, then it became common until it became part of their speech. He explained this by saying that this plural, since it is pluralised (again), as they said: "sawahibat Yusuf" and "nawakisi al-absar," resembled the singular, so tanwin was applied to it. One of the rajaz poets said:

"Tanwin in the plural has come frequently, until a people claimed with it the option."

The tanwin is established in the mushafs of Madina, Makka, Kufa and Basra, and in the mushafs of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah; likewise "qawarir." Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: "salasila" in continuation, and "salasila" with an alif without tanwin in pause. It is also reported that among the Arabs there are those who say: "ra'aytu 'Amra" with the alif in pause.

﴿مِن كَأْسٍ﴾ (from a cup): "min" indicates the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). ﴿كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾ (its mixture is camphor). Qatada said: It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It is also said that this is by way of comparison, meaning: fragrant of smell and coolness like camphor. Al-Kalbi said: "Kafuran" is the name of a spring in Paradise, and it was given tanwin to match the verse-endings. 'Abd Allah read "qafuran" with qaf in place of kaf; these two often interchange within a word, as in the saying: "'arabi quhhun" and "kuhhun" (pure Arab).

"'Aynan" is a substitute for "kafuran" and an object of ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ﴾ (they drink), meaning: water of a spring; or it is a substitute from the position of "min ka's" with an elided noun, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring; or it is put in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas). Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. He used the "ba'" which indicates joining (al-ilsaq), and the meaning: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, as you say: "I drank water with honey." Or "yashrabu" is taken to imply "yarwa" (to quench), and so it takes "ba'". It is also said: the "ba'" is extra and the meaning is "yashrabu biha"; al-Hudhali said:

"They drank the water of the sea, then they rose, and to them, in the upper reaches of green seas, is a groaning."

It was said: that is, they drank the water of the sea. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yashraba-ha."

﴿عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾ (the servants of Allah) here are the believers. ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها﴾ (they cause it to gush): they pierce it with a cane stalk or the like wherever they wish, so it flows for each one of them; this is how it is reported in the narration. It is also said: it is a spring in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that gushes out to the houses of the prophets and the believers.

﴿يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ﴾ (they fulfil the vow) in this world, and they used to fear. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿يُوفُونَ﴾ is the answer to one who might say: "Why are they given that?" End of quote. Thus he used "'asa" as a relative for "man," which is not permissible, and after "'asa" he used the present tense not preceded by "an," which is rare or found only in poetry. The apparent meaning is that "nadhr" refers to what is well known in the Sharia as a vow. Al-Asamm, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being diligent in performing obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself will be more faithful to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon him. It is also said: the "nadhr" here is general, covering what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory and what the servant has made obligatory upon himself, so faith and all acts of obedience are included in it.

﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. The first is more praiseworthy, because it involves preferring others over oneself; as for the second, the wealthy may do it more often. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is a captive from the people of the qibla. It is said: "wa-asiran" is a metaphor and a figure of speech. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is the imprisoned person. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."

﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾ (We feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance): this is by implying a saying (idmar al-qawl). It is permissible that they declared it explicitly, addressing those mentioned, to prevent them from reciprocating with the like or with thanks, since their kindness is done for the countenance of Allah the Exalted, so there is no sense in repaying the creation; and this is the apparent meaning. Mujahid said: As for them, they did not speak it, but Allah the Exalted knew it from them, so He praised them for it.

﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. This verse was said to have been revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face. Al-Naqqash mentioned in this a very long narrative, apparently full of disagreement; in it there is an indication for the needy, the orphan and the captive, who are addressed with it in the house of prophethood, and an indication for Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, who addresses each of them; its outward form is disagreement, due to the baseness of its wording, the breaking of its verses and the triviality of its meanings.

﴿يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا﴾ (a stern day): attributing sternness to the day is a metaphor. Ibn 'Abbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from his eyes like tar. The majority read ﴿فَوَقاهُمُ﴾ (so Allah will protect them) with a light qaf; Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled.

﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." It is also said: they will not see in it a sun or a moon, and "al-zamharir" in the dialect of Tayy is the moon.

The majority read ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ (and near). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) coordinated with ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ (reclining). He also said: it is permissible that it be an attribute of the garden, so the meaning is: and He recompensed them with a near garden. Al-Zamakhshari said, in meaning, that it is a circumstantial state coordinated upon another state, which is "la yarawna" (they will not see), that is, not seeing; the waw entered to indicate that both matters are combined for them, as if it were said: and He recompensed them with a garden in which they combine between distance from heat and cold and the nearness of the shades over them. Abu Haywa read "wa-daniyatun" with raf', and al-Akhfash used it as evidence for the permissibility of raising the active participle without its being preceded by a dependent, such as your saying: "qa'imun al-zaydun" (standing are the Zaydun); but there is no proof in it, because the more apparent reading is that ﴿ظِلالُها﴾ (its shades) is the subject and ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ is its predicate. Al-A'mash read "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," which is like His saying: ﴿خاشِعَةً أبْصارُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes humbled) [al-Ma'arij: 44]. Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Dahr is Medinan and has thirty-one verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, which We test; and We made him hearing and seeing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor,﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly.﴾ ﴿They fulfil their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾ ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive.﴾ ﴿"We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not desire from you reward or thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is frowning and distressing."﴾ ﴿So Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and will give them radiance and joy.﴾ ﴿And He will reward them, for what they endured, with a garden and silk.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein on couches, they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold.﴾ ﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in submission.﴾.

This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Mujahid and Qatadah said it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said it is Medinan except for one verse, which is Meccan, namely: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. It was also said that it is Medinan except for His words: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 24] and so on, for this is Meccan; this was related by al-Mawardi. Its connection to what precedes it is very clear and needs no explanation.

(Hal) is an interrogative particle. If it enters upon a nominal sentence, it cannot be interpreted as qad (indeed, already), because qad is one of the distinguishing features of the verb. If it enters upon a verb, it most commonly comes for pure interrogation. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said that here it has the meaning of qad. It was said: this is because the original form was (ahal), so the hamzah was dropped and the particle alone was used for interrogation. This is shown by the verse:

*"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about their encampment: did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, which has hills?"*

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come upon man, a short time ago, a period of time, approximately and generally, in which he was not such-and-such?" The answer then is: "It came upon him while he was in the state mentioned." It was recited in the presence of Abu Bakr, or it was said in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "I wish it had been completed," meaning: I wish that state had been completed, namely that he was a thing not worth mentioning, not yet created and not yet obligated.

Here "man" (al-insan) refers to the whole species of the children of Adam. The period of time that passed over him was either the time of his non-existence or the time of his being a drop of sperm. His movement from one stage to another, until the time when he could be addressed, is a period in which he had no mention; he is called "man" by reference to what he became. It was also said: the one meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and the period that passed over him is the duration in which he remained until the spirit was breathed into him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he remained as clay for forty years, then as dried clay for forty years, then as black mud moulded for forty years, so his creation was completed in one hundred and twenty years, and he is called "man" by reference to what he came to be.

The clause "he was not" (lam yakun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "man," as if it were said: "not worth mentioning." This is the apparent meaning. Or it is in the position of an attributive clause (sifa) for "a period" (hin), in which case the returning pronoun referring to the modified noun is omitted, meaning: "he was not in it."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: he is the species of the children of Adam, because Adam was not created from a sperm-drop. ﴿A mixture﴾: that is, a combination of ingredients, and it is an attribute of the sperm-drop. Ibn Mas'ud and Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father, said: they are the veins that are in the sperm-drop. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it is the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, which mixed in the womb, and man was created from both of them. Al-Hasan said: it is the mixing of the sperm-drop with menstrual blood, for when a woman conceives, menstruation stops. Ibn 'Abbas also, along with 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, said: they are mixtures moving from a sperm-drop to a clot, to a lump of flesh, and to other stages, until man is brought into being. "'Aynan" is a substitute for "kafuran" and an object of ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ﴾ (they drink), meaning: water of a spring; or it is a substitute from the position of "min ka's" with an elided noun, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring; or it is put in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas). Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. He used the "ba'" which indicates joining (al-ilsaq), and the meaning: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, as you say: "I drank water with honey." Or "yashrabu" is taken to imply "yarwa" (to quench), and so it takes "ba'". It is also said: the "ba'" is extra and the meaning is "yashrabu biha"; al-Hudhali said:

"They drank the water of the sea, then they rose, and to them, in the upper reaches of green seas, is a groaning."

It was said: that is, they drank the water of the sea. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yashraba-ha."

﴿عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾ (the servants of Allah) here are the believers. ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها﴾ (they cause it to gush): they pierce it with a cane stalk or the like wherever they wish, so it flows for each one of them; this is how it is reported in the narration. It is also said: it is a spring in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that gushes out to the houses of the prophets and the believers.

﴿يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ﴾ (they fulfil the vow) in this world, and they used to fear. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿يُوفُونَ﴾ is the answer to one who might say: "Why are they given that?" End of quote. Thus he used "'asa" as a relative for "man," which is not permissible, and after "'asa" he used the present tense not preceded by "an," which is rare or found only in poetry. The apparent meaning is that "nadhr" refers to what is well known in the Sharia as a vow. Al-Asamm, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being diligent in performing obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself will be more faithful to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon him. It is also said: the "nadhr" here is general, covering what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory and what the servant has made obligatory upon himself, so faith and all acts of obedience are included in it.

﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. The first is more praiseworthy, because it involves preferring others over oneself; as for the second, the wealthy may do it more often. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is a captive from the people of the qibla. It is said: "wa-asiran" is a metaphor and a figure of speech. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is the imprisoned person. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."

﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾ (We feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance): this is by implying a saying (idmar al-qawl). It is permissible that they declared it explicitly, addressing those mentioned, to prevent them from reciprocating with the like or with thanks, since their kindness is done for the countenance of Allah the Exalted, so there is no sense in repaying the creation; and this is the apparent meaning. Mujahid said: As for them, they did not speak it, but Allah the Exalted knew it from them, so He praised them for it.

﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. This verse was said to have been revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face. Al-Naqqash mentioned in this a very long narrative, apparently full of disagreement; in it there is an indication for the needy, the orphan and the captive, who are addressed with it in the house of prophethood, and an indication for Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, who addresses each of them; its outward form is disagreement, due to the baseness of its wording, the breaking of its verses and the triviality of its meanings.

﴿يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا﴾ (a stern day): attributing sternness to the day is a metaphor. Ibn 'Abbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from his eyes like tar. The majority read ﴿فَوَقاهُمُ﴾ (so Allah will protect them) with a light qaf; Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled.

﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." It is also said: they will not see in it a sun or a moon, and "al-zamharir" in the dialect of Tayy is the moon.

The majority read ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ (and near). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) coordinated with ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ (reclining). He also said: it is permissible that it be an attribute of the garden, so the meaning is: and He recompensed them with a near garden. Al-Zamakhshari said, in meaning, that it is a circumstantial state coordinated upon another state, which is "la yarawna" (they will not see), that is, not seeing; the waw entered to indicate that both matters are combined for them, as if it were said: and He recompensed them with a garden in which they combine between distance from heat and cold and the nearness of the shades over them. Abu Haywa read "wa-daniyatun" with raf', and al-Akhfash used it as evidence for the permissibility of raising the active participle without its being preceded by a dependent, such as your saying: "qa'imun al-zaydun" (standing are the Zaydun); but there is no proof in it, because the more apparent reading is that ﴿ظِلالُها﴾ (its shades) is the subject and ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ is its predicate. Al-A'mash read "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," which is like His saying: ﴿خاشِعَةً أبْصارُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes humbled) [al-Ma'arij: 44]. Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Dahr is Medinan and has thirty-one verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, which We test; and We made him hearing and seeing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor,﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly.﴾ ﴿They fulfil their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾ ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive.﴾ ﴿"We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not desire from you reward or thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is frowning and distressing."﴾ ﴿So Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and will give them radiance and joy.﴾ ﴿And He will reward them, for what they endured, with a garden and silk.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein on couches, they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold.﴾ ﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in submission.﴾.

This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Mujahid and Qatadah said it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said it is Medinan except for one verse, which is Meccan, namely: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. It was also said that it is Medinan except for His words: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 24] and so on, for this is Meccan; this was related by al-Mawardi. Its connection to what precedes it is very clear and needs no explanation.

(Hal) is an interrogative particle. If it enters upon a nominal sentence, it cannot be interpreted as qad (indeed, already), because qad is one of the distinguishing features of the verb. If it enters upon a verb, it most commonly comes for pure interrogation. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said that here it has the meaning of qad. It was said: this is because the original form was (ahal), so the hamzah was dropped and the particle alone was used for interrogation. This is shown by the verse:

*"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about their encampment: did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, which has hills?"*

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come upon man, a short time ago, a period of time, approximately and generally, in which he was not such-and-such?" The answer then is: "It came upon him while he was in the state mentioned." It was recited in the presence of Abu Bakr, or it was said in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "I wish it had been completed," meaning: I wish that state had been completed, namely that he was a thing not worth mentioning, not yet created and not yet obligated.

Here "man" (al-insan) refers to the whole species of the children of Adam. The period of time that passed over him was either the time of his non-existence or the time of his being a drop of sperm. His movement from one stage to another, until the time when he could be addressed, is a period in which he had no mention; he is called "man" by reference to what he became. It was also said: the one meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and the period that passed over him is the duration in which he remained until the spirit was breathed into him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he remained as clay for forty years, then as dried clay for forty years, then as black mud moulded for forty years, so his creation was completed in one hundred and twenty years, and he is called "man" by reference to what he came to be.

The clause "he was not" (lam yakun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "man," as if it were said: "not worth mentioning." This is the apparent meaning. Or it is in the position of an attributive clause (sifa) for "a period" (hin), in which case the returning pronoun referring to the modified noun is omitted, meaning: "he was not in it."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: he is the species of the children of Adam, because Adam was not created from a sperm-drop. ﴿A mixture﴾: that is, a combination of ingredients, and it is an attribute of the sperm-drop. Ibn Mas'ud and Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father, said: they are the veins that are in the sperm-drop. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it is the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, which mixed in the womb, and man was created from both of them. Al-Hasan said: it is the mixing of the sperm-drop with menstrual blood, for when a woman conceives, menstruation stops. Ibn 'Abbas also, along with 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, said: they are mixtures moving from a sperm-drop to a clot, to a lump of flesh, and to other stages, until man is brought into being. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with al-Kalbi, said: they are the colours of the sperm-drop. It was said: they are mixtures of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The sperm-drop is intended as a species, which is why it is described with a plural, like His words: ﴿on green cushions﴾ [al-Rahman: 76]; or because each part of the sperm-drop is treated as a sperm-drop.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "sperm-drop mixture" (nutfatin amshaj) is like "a cooking pot of firewood" (burmatin a'sar) and "a garment of fibres" (burdin akyas), and these are singular nouns which are not plurals, which is why they occur as attributes of singulars. It is also said: "a sperm-drop of mashaj" (nutfatu mashajin), and amshaj cannot be a broken plural of it; rather, both are equal in being singular, since a singular is described by them. End of quote. His statement contradicts the explicit text of Sibawayh and the grammarians that af'al (the pattern of amshaj) does not occur as a singular. Sibawayh said: "There is no af'al in speech except that it is broken from a noun which functions as a collective; and whatever is reported of a singular being described by af'al, they have interpreted it."

﴿We test him﴾: We examine him through legal obligation in this world. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: We turn him about in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop and then a clot. According to this view, the clause is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (hal musahiba). According to the view that the meaning is testing him by obligation, it is a future circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because when He created him from a sperm-drop, He was not yet testing him with obligation at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also mean that We move him from one state to another, and that testing has been called such by way of metaphor. End of quote. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement. It was also said: We test him with the creation and existence in this world, so it is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech; the original order is: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾, while "We test him" follows; that is, making him hearing and seeing is the testing. There is no need to claim inversion, and the meaning is sound without it. He bestowed upon him a favour by making him with these two attributes, and they are an allusion to discernment and understanding, since their instruments are the cause of that; and they are the noblest of the senses, by which the greatest things are perceived.

When He had made him in this condition, He informed that He guided him to the way, that is: He directed him to the path and made known to him the outcome of the path of salvation and the outcome of the path of destruction, since He directed him to the path of guidance. Mujahid said: the way of happiness and misery. Al-Suddi said: the way out of the womb. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We enabled him and empowered him in both his states; and when We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, it was known from Him that he would either believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof. End of quote, and this is according to the method of entailment (iltizam).

The majority read (imma) with a kasra on the hamzah in both places. Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-'Aj, who is Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sulami, a Syrian who was governor of Basra for Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, read it with a fatha in both places. This is a dialect related by Abu Zayd from the Arabs, and it is the one that some people counted among the conjunctions (huruf al-'atf). They recited:

*"There will overtake her either a harsh north wind, or the blowing of an east wind at the end of the evening."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a good reading, and the meaning is: either grateful, by Our guidance, or ungrateful, through his own bad choice. End of quote. He made "إمّا" (imma) the detailed (tafsili) particle that carries the sense of a condition, which is why it is followed by the particle of response (fa'), so it becomes like the Arabs' saying: "Imma sadiqan fa-sadiqun" (either a friend, then a friend). "Shakiran" and "kafuran" are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the pronoun of object in ﴿هَدَيْناهُ﴾ (We guided him). Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that they be two states of "al-sabil" (the way), meaning: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ (And We guided him to the two highways) [al-Balad: 10], where He described the way with gratitude and disbelief figuratively. End of quote. Since few people are characterised by gratitude, He said "shakiran" (grateful). Since disbelief is common, and many people are characterised by it, and its occurrence from man is frequent, unlike gratitude, He came with "kafuran" in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). When He mentioned the two groups, He followed them with the threat and the promise.

Talha, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ (salasila) without tanwin (diptote) both in pause and in continuation. It is reported from Hamza and Abu 'Amr that in pause they used the alif. Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan read it without tanwin, and there is difference of transmission from them regarding pause, and likewise from al-Bazzi. The remaining seven read it with tanwin in continuation, and with the alif replacing it in pause; this is the reading of al-A'mash. It is said: This is according to what al-Akhfash related of the dialect of those who give tanwin to every word that is not declined except "af'al min", and this is the dialect of the poets, then it became common until it became part of their speech. He explained this by saying that this plural, since it is pluralised (again), as they said: "sawahibat Yusuf" and "nawakisi al-absar," resembled the singular, so tanwin was applied to it. One of the rajaz poets said:

"Tanwin in the plural has come frequently, until a people claimed with it the option."

The tanwin is established in the mushafs of Madina, Makka, Kufa and Basra, and in the mushafs of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah; likewise "qawarir." Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: "salasila" in continuation, and "salasila" with an alif without tanwin in pause. It is also reported that among the Arabs there are those who say: "ra'aytu 'Amra" with the alif in pause.

﴿مِن كَأْسٍ﴾ (from a cup): "min" indicates the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). ﴿كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾ (its mixture is camphor). Qatada said: It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It is also said that this is by way of comparison, meaning: fragrant of smell and coolness like camphor. Al-Kalbi said: "Kafuran" is the name of a spring in Paradise, and it was given tanwin to match the verse-endings. Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. ﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."
