﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. This verse was said to have been revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face. Al-Naqqash mentioned in this a very long narrative, apparently full of disagreement; in it there is an indication for the needy, the orphan and the captive, who are addressed with it in the house of prophethood, and an indication for Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, who addresses each of them; its outward form is disagreement, due to the baseness of its wording, the breaking of its verses and the triviality of its meanings.

﴿يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا﴾ (a stern day): attributing sternness to the day is a metaphor. Ibn 'Abbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from his eyes like tar. The majority read ﴿فَوَقاهُمُ﴾ (so Allah will protect them) with a light qaf; Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled.

﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." It is also said: they will not see in it a sun or a moon, and "al-zamharir" in the dialect of Tayy is the moon.

The majority read ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ (and near). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) coordinated with ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ (reclining). He also said: it is permissible that it be an attribute of the garden, so the meaning is: and He recompensed them with a near garden. Al-Zamakhshari said, in meaning, that it is a circumstantial state coordinated upon another state, which is "la yarawna" (they will not see), that is, not seeing; the waw entered to indicate that both matters are combined for them, as if it were said: and He recompensed them with a garden in which they combine between distance from heat and cold and the nearness of the shades over them. Abu Haywa read "wa-daniyatun" with raf', and al-Akhfash used it as evidence for the permissibility of raising the active participle without its being preceded by a dependent, such as your saying: "qa'imun al-zaydun" (standing are the Zaydun); but there is no proof in it, because the more apparent reading is that ﴿ظِلالُها﴾ (its shades) is the subject and ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ is its predicate. Al-A'mash read "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," which is like His saying: ﴿خاشِعَةً أبْصارُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes humbled) [al-Ma'arij: 44]. Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Dahr is Medinan and has thirty-one verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, which We test; and We made him hearing and seeing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor,﴾ ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it gush forth abundantly.﴾ ﴿They fulfil their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾ ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive.﴾ ﴿"We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not desire from you reward or thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day that is frowning and distressing."﴾ ﴿So Allah will protect them from the evil of that Day and will give them radiance and joy.﴾ ﴿And He will reward them, for what they endured, with a garden and silk.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein on couches, they will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold.﴾ ﴿And near over them will be its shade, and its clusters will be lowered in submission.﴾.

This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Mujahid and Qatadah said it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said it is Medinan except for one verse, which is Meccan, namely: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan: 24]. It was also said that it is Medinan except for His words: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 24] and so on, for this is Meccan; this was related by al-Mawardi. Its connection to what precedes it is very clear and needs no explanation.

(Hal) is an interrogative particle. If it enters upon a nominal sentence, it cannot be interpreted as qad (indeed, already), because qad is one of the distinguishing features of the verb. If it enters upon a verb, it most commonly comes for pure interrogation. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said that here it has the meaning of qad. It was said: this is because the original form was (ahal), so the hamzah was dropped and the particle alone was used for interrogation. This is shown by the verse:

*"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about their encampment: did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, which has hills?"*

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come upon man, a short time ago, a period of time, approximately and generally, in which he was not such-and-such?" The answer then is: "It came upon him while he was in the state mentioned." It was recited in the presence of Abu Bakr, or it was said in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "I wish it had been completed," meaning: I wish that state had been completed, namely that he was a thing not worth mentioning, not yet created and not yet obligated.

Here "man" (al-insan) refers to the whole species of the children of Adam. The period of time that passed over him was either the time of his non-existence or the time of his being a drop of sperm. His movement from one stage to another, until the time when he could be addressed, is a period in which he had no mention; he is called "man" by reference to what he became. It was also said: the one meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and the period that passed over him is the duration in which he remained until the spirit was breathed into him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he remained as clay for forty years, then as dried clay for forty years, then as black mud moulded for forty years, so his creation was completed in one hundred and twenty years, and he is called "man" by reference to what he came to be.

The clause "he was not" (lam yakun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "man," as if it were said: "not worth mentioning." This is the apparent meaning. Or it is in the position of an attributive clause (sifa) for "a period" (hin), in which case the returning pronoun referring to the modified noun is omitted, meaning: "he was not in it."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: he is the species of the children of Adam, because Adam was not created from a sperm-drop. ﴿A mixture﴾: that is, a combination of ingredients, and it is an attribute of the sperm-drop. Ibn Mas'ud and Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father, said: they are the veins that are in the sperm-drop. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it is the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, which mixed in the womb, and man was created from both of them. Al-Hasan said: it is the mixing of the sperm-drop with menstrual blood, for when a woman conceives, menstruation stops. Ibn 'Abbas also, along with 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, said: they are mixtures moving from a sperm-drop to a clot, to a lump of flesh, and to other stages, until man is brought into being. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with al-Kalbi, said: they are the colours of the sperm-drop. It was said: they are mixtures of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The sperm-drop is intended as a species, which is why it is described with a plural, like His words: ﴿on green cushions﴾ [al-Rahman: 76]; or because each part of the sperm-drop is treated as a sperm-drop.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "sperm-drop mixture" (nutfatin amshaj) is like "a cooking pot of firewood" (burmatin a'sar) and "a garment of fibres" (burdin akyas), and these are singular nouns which are not plurals, which is why they occur as attributes of singulars. It is also said: "a sperm-drop of mashaj" (nutfatu mashajin), and amshaj cannot be a broken plural of it; rather, both are equal in being singular, since a singular is described by them. End of quote. His statement contradicts the explicit text of Sibawayh and the grammarians that af'al (the pattern of amshaj) does not occur as a singular. Sibawayh said: "There is no af'al in speech except that it is broken from a noun which functions as a collective; and whatever is reported of a singular being described by af'al, they have interpreted it."

﴿We test him﴾: We examine him through legal obligation in this world. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: We turn him about in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop and then a clot. According to this view, the clause is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (hal musahiba). According to the view that the meaning is testing him by obligation, it is a future circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because when He created him from a sperm-drop, He was not yet testing him with obligation at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also mean that We move him from one state to another, and that testing has been called such by way of metaphor. End of quote. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement. It was also said: We test him with the creation and existence in this world, so it is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech; the original order is: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾, while "We test him" follows; that is, making him hearing and seeing is the testing. There is no need to claim inversion, and the meaning is sound without it. He bestowed upon him a favour by making him with these two attributes, and they are an allusion to discernment and understanding, since their instruments are the cause of that; and they are the noblest of the senses, by which the greatest things are perceived.

When He had made him in this condition, He informed that He guided him to the way, that is: He directed him to the path and made known to him the outcome of the path of salvation and the outcome of the path of destruction, since He directed him to the path of guidance. Mujahid said: the way of happiness and misery. Al-Suddi said: the way out of the womb. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We enabled him and empowered him in both his states; and when We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, it was known from Him that he would either believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof. End of quote, and this is according to the method of entailment (iltizam).

The majority read (imma) with a kasra on the hamzah in both places. Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-'Aj, who is Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sulami, a Syrian who was governor of Basra for Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, read it with a fatha in both places. This is a dialect related by Abu Zayd from the Arabs, and it is the one that some people counted among the conjunctions (huruf al-'atf). They recited:

*"There will overtake her either a harsh north wind, or the blowing of an east wind at the end of the evening."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a good reading, and the meaning is: either grateful, by Our guidance, or ungrateful, through his own bad choice. End of quote. He made "إمّا" (imma) the detailed (tafsili) particle that carries the sense of a condition, which is why it is followed by the particle of response (fa'), so it becomes like the Arabs' saying: "Imma sadiqan fa-sadiqun" (either a friend, then a friend). "Shakiran" and "kafuran" are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the pronoun of object in ﴿هَدَيْناهُ﴾ (We guided him). Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that they be two states of "al-sabil" (the way), meaning: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ (And We guided him to the two highways) [al-Balad: 10], where He described the way with gratitude and disbelief figuratively. End of quote. Since few people are characterised by gratitude, He said "shakiran" (grateful). Since disbelief is common, and many people are characterised by it, and its occurrence from man is frequent, unlike gratitude, He came with "kafuran" in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). When He mentioned the two groups, He followed them with the threat and the promise.

Talha, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ (salasila) without tanwin (diptote) both in pause and in continuation. It is reported from Hamza and Abu 'Amr that in pause they used the alif. Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan read it without tanwin, and there is difference of transmission from them regarding pause, and likewise from al-Bazzi. The remaining seven read it with tanwin in continuation, and with the alif replacing it in pause; this is the reading of al-A'mash. It is said: This is according to what al-Akhfash related of the dialect of those who give tanwin to every word that is not declined except "af'al min", and this is the dialect of the poets, then it became common until it became part of their speech. He explained this by saying that this plural, since it is pluralised (again), as they said: "sawahibat Yusuf" and "nawakisi al-absar," resembled the singular, so tanwin was applied to it. One of the rajaz poets said:

"Tanwin in the plural has come frequently, until a people claimed with it the option."

The tanwin is established in the mushafs of Madina, Makka, Kufa and Basra, and in the mushafs of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah; likewise "qawarir." Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: "salasila" in continuation, and "salasila" with an alif without tanwin in pause. It is also reported that among the Arabs there are those who say: "ra'aytu 'Amra" with the alif in pause.

﴿مِن كَأْسٍ﴾ (from a cup): "min" indicates the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). ﴿كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾ (its mixture is camphor). Qatada said: It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It is also said that this is by way of comparison, meaning: fragrant of smell and coolness like camphor. Al-Kalbi said: "Kafuran" is the name of a spring in Paradise, and it was given tanwin to match the verse-endings. 'Abd Allah read "qafuran" with qaf in place of kaf; these two often interchange within a word, as in the saying: "'arabi quhhun" and "kuhhun" (pure Arab).

"'Aynan" is a substitute for "kafuran" and an object of ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ﴾ (they drink), meaning: water of a spring; or it is a substitute from the position of "min ka's" with an elided noun, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring; or it is put in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas). Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. He used the "ba'" which indicates joining (al-ilsaq), and the meaning: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, as you say: "I drank water with honey." Or "yashrabu" is taken to imply "yarwa" (to quench), and so it takes "ba'". It is also said: the "ba'" is extra and the meaning is "yashrabu biha"; al-Hudhali said:

"They drank the water of the sea, then they rose, and to them, in the upper reaches of green seas, is a groaning."

It was said: that is, they drank the water of the sea. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yashraba-ha."

﴿عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾ (the servants of Allah) here are the believers. ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها﴾ (they cause it to gush): they pierce it with a cane stalk or the like wherever they wish, so it flows for each one of them; this is how it is reported in the narration. It is also said: it is a spring in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that gushes out to the houses of the prophets and the believers.

﴿يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ﴾ (they fulfil the vow) in this world, and they used to fear. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿يُوفُونَ﴾ is the answer to one who might say: "Why are they given that?" End of quote. Thus he used "'asa" as a relative for "man," which is not permissible, and after "'asa" he used the present tense not preceded by "an," which is rare or found only in poetry. The apparent meaning is that "nadhr" refers to what is well known in the Sharia as a vow. Al-Asamm, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being diligent in performing obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself will be more faithful to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon him. It is also said: the "nadhr" here is general, covering what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory and what the servant has made obligatory upon himself, so faith and all acts of obedience are included in it.

﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. The first is more praiseworthy, because it involves preferring others over oneself; as for the second, the wealthy may do it more often. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is a captive from the people of the qibla. It is said: "wa-asiran" is a metaphor and a figure of speech. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is the imprisoned person. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."

﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾ (We feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance): this is by implying a saying (idmar al-qawl). It is permissible that they declared it explicitly, addressing those mentioned, to prevent them from reciprocating with the like or with thanks, since their kindness is done for the countenance of Allah the Exalted, so there is no sense in repaying the creation; and this is the apparent meaning. Mujahid said: As for them, they did not speak it, but Allah the Exalted knew it from them, so He praised them for it.

﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. ﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. (Hal) is an interrogative particle. If it enters upon a nominal sentence, it cannot be interpreted as qad (indeed, already), because qad is one of the distinguishing features of the verb. If it enters upon a verb, it most commonly comes for pure interrogation. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said that here it has the meaning of qad. It was said: this is because the original form was (ahal), so the hamzah was dropped and the particle alone was used for interrogation. This is shown by the verse:

*"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about their encampment: did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, which has hills?"*

So the meaning is: "Has there indeed come upon man, a short time ago, a period of time, approximately and generally, in which he was not such-and-such?" The answer then is: "It came upon him while he was in the state mentioned." It was recited in the presence of Abu Bakr, or it was said in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "I wish it had been completed," meaning: I wish that state had been completed, namely that he was a thing not worth mentioning, not yet created and not yet obligated.

Here "man" (al-insan) refers to the whole species of the children of Adam. The period of time that passed over him was either the time of his non-existence or the time of his being a drop of sperm. His movement from one stage to another, until the time when he could be addressed, is a period in which he had no mention; he is called "man" by reference to what he became. It was also said: the one meant is Adam, peace be upon him, and the period that passed over him is the duration in which he remained until the spirit was breathed into him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he remained as clay for forty years, then as dried clay for forty years, then as black mud moulded for forty years, so his creation was completed in one hundred and twenty years, and he is called "man" by reference to what he came to be.

The clause "he was not" (lam yakun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "man," as if it were said: "not worth mentioning." This is the apparent meaning. Or it is in the position of an attributive clause (sifa) for "a period" (hin), in which case the returning pronoun referring to the modified noun is omitted, meaning: "he was not in it."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: he is the species of the children of Adam, because Adam was not created from a sperm-drop. ﴿A mixture﴾: that is, a combination of ingredients, and it is an attribute of the sperm-drop. Ibn Mas'ud and Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father, said: they are the veins that are in the sperm-drop. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it is the semen of the man and the semen of the woman, which mixed in the womb, and man was created from both of them. Al-Hasan said: it is the mixing of the sperm-drop with menstrual blood, for when a woman conceives, menstruation stops. Ibn 'Abbas also, along with 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, said: they are mixtures moving from a sperm-drop to a clot, to a lump of flesh, and to other stages, until man is brought into being. Ibn 'Abbas also, together with al-Kalbi, said: they are the colours of the sperm-drop. It was said: they are mixtures of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The sperm-drop is intended as a species, which is why it is described with a plural, like His words: ﴿on green cushions﴾ [al-Rahman: 76]; or because each part of the sperm-drop is treated as a sperm-drop.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "sperm-drop mixture" (nutfatin amshaj) is like "a cooking pot of firewood" (burmatin a'sar) and "a garment of fibres" (burdin akyas), and these are singular nouns which are not plurals, which is why they occur as attributes of singulars. It is also said: "a sperm-drop of mashaj" (nutfatu mashajin), and amshaj cannot be a broken plural of it; rather, both are equal in being singular, since a singular is described by them. End of quote. His statement contradicts the explicit text of Sibawayh and the grammarians that af'al (the pattern of amshaj) does not occur as a singular. Sibawayh said: "There is no af'al in speech except that it is broken from a noun which functions as a collective; and whatever is reported of a singular being described by af'al, they have interpreted it."

﴿We test him﴾: We examine him through legal obligation in this world. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: We turn him about in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop and then a clot. According to this view, the clause is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause (hal musahiba). According to the view that the meaning is testing him by obligation, it is a future circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because when He created him from a sperm-drop, He was not yet testing him with obligation at that time. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also mean that We move him from one state to another, and that testing has been called such by way of metaphor. End of quote. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement. It was also said: We test him with the creation and existence in this world, so it is a contemporaneous circumstantial clause. It was also said: there is inversion in the speech; the original order is: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾, while "We test him" follows; that is, making him hearing and seeing is the testing. There is no need to claim inversion, and the meaning is sound without it. He bestowed upon him a favour by making him with these two attributes, and they are an allusion to discernment and understanding, since their instruments are the cause of that; and they are the noblest of the senses, by which the greatest things are perceived.

When He had made him in this condition, He informed that He guided him to the way, that is: He directed him to the path and made known to him the outcome of the path of salvation and the outcome of the path of destruction, since He directed him to the path of guidance. Mujahid said: the way of happiness and misery. Al-Suddi said: the way out of the womb. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, We enabled him and empowered him in both his states; and when We called him to Islam through the proofs of reason and revelation, it was known from Him that he would either believe or disbelieve, in order to establish the proof. End of quote, and this is according to the method of entailment (iltizam).

The majority read (imma) with a kasra on the hamzah in both places. Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-'Aj, who is Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Sulami, a Syrian who was governor of Basra for Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, read it with a fatha in both places. This is a dialect related by Abu Zayd from the Arabs, and it is the one that some people counted among the conjunctions (huruf al-'atf). They recited:

*"There will overtake her either a harsh north wind, or the blowing of an east wind at the end of the evening."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a good reading, and the meaning is: either grateful, by Our guidance, or ungrateful, through his own bad choice. End of quote. He made "إمّا" (imma) the detailed (tafsili) particle that carries the sense of a condition, which is why it is followed by the particle of response (fa'), so it becomes like the Arabs' saying: "Imma sadiqan fa-sadiqun" (either a friend, then a friend). "Shakiran" and "kafuran" are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of the pronoun of object in ﴿هَدَيْناهُ﴾ (We guided him). Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is permissible that they be two states of "al-sabil" (the way), meaning: We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, like His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ (And We guided him to the two highways) [al-Balad: 10], where He described the way with gratitude and disbelief figuratively. End of quote. Since few people are characterised by gratitude, He said "shakiran" (grateful). Since disbelief is common, and many people are characterised by it, and its occurrence from man is frequent, unlike gratitude, He came with "kafuran" in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). When He mentioned the two groups, He followed them with the threat and the promise.

Talha, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ (salasila) without tanwin (diptote) both in pause and in continuation. It is reported from Hamza and Abu 'Amr that in pause they used the alif. Hafs and Ibn Dhakwan read it without tanwin, and there is difference of transmission from them regarding pause, and likewise from al-Bazzi. The remaining seven read it with tanwin in continuation, and with the alif replacing it in pause; this is the reading of al-A'mash. It is said: This is according to what al-Akhfash related of the dialect of those who give tanwin to every word that is not declined except "af'al min", and this is the dialect of the poets, then it became common until it became part of their speech. He explained this by saying that this plural, since it is pluralised (again), as they said: "sawahibat Yusuf" and "nawakisi al-absar," resembled the singular, so tanwin was applied to it. One of the rajaz poets said:

"Tanwin in the plural has come frequently, until a people claimed with it the option."

The tanwin is established in the mushafs of Madina, Makka, Kufa and Basra, and in the mushafs of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah; likewise "qawarir." Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: "salasila" in continuation, and "salasila" with an alif without tanwin in pause. It is also reported that among the Arabs there are those who say: "ra'aytu 'Amra" with the alif in pause.

﴿مِن كَأْسٍ﴾ (from a cup): "min" indicates the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). ﴿كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾ (its mixture is camphor). Qatada said: It is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It is also said that this is by way of comparison, meaning: fragrant of smell and coolness like camphor. Al-Kalbi said: "Kafuran" is the name of a spring in Paradise, and it was given tanwin to match the verse-endings. 'Abd Allah read "qafuran" with qaf in place of kaf; these two often interchange within a word, as in the saying: "'arabi quhhun" and "kuhhun" (pure Arab).

"'Aynan" is a substitute for "kafuran" and an object of ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ﴾ (they drink), meaning: water of a spring; or it is a substitute from the position of "min ka's" with an elided noun, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring; or it is put in the accusative by specification (al-ikhtisas). Since the cup is the starting point of their drinking, He used "min" and "fi".

﴿يَشْرَبُ بِها﴾ (drink with it), that is: their drink is mixed with it. He used the "ba'" which indicates joining (al-ilsaq), and the meaning: the servants of Allah drink wine with it, as you say: "I drank water with honey." Or "yashrabu" is taken to imply "yarwa" (to quench), and so it takes "ba'". It is also said: the "ba'" is extra and the meaning is "yashrabu biha"; al-Hudhali said:

"They drank the water of the sea, then they rose, and to them, in the upper reaches of green seas, is a groaning."

It was said: that is, they drank the water of the sea. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yashraba-ha."

﴿عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾ (the servants of Allah) here are the believers. ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها﴾ (they cause it to gush): they pierce it with a cane stalk or the like wherever they wish, so it flows for each one of them; this is how it is reported in the narration. It is also said: it is a spring in the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that gushes out to the houses of the prophets and the believers.

﴿يُوفُونَ بِالنَّذْرِ﴾ (they fulfil the vow) in this world, and they used to fear. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿يُوفُونَ﴾ is the answer to one who might say: "Why are they given that?" End of quote. Thus he used "'asa" as a relative for "man," which is not permissible, and after "'asa" he used the present tense not preceded by "an," which is rare or found only in poetry. The apparent meaning is that "nadhr" refers to what is well known in the Sharia as a vow. Al-Asamm, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being diligent in performing obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself will be more faithful to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon him. It is also said: the "nadhr" here is general, covering what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory and what the servant has made obligatory upon himself, so faith and all acts of obedience are included in it.

﴿عَلى حُبِّهِ﴾ (upon His love): that is, upon love of food, since it is loved for poverty and need; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Or "upon the love of Allah," that is, for His sake and seeking His pleasure; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani. The first is more praiseworthy, because it involves preferring others over oneself; as for the second, the wealthy may do it more often. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "upon love of food," meaning: they are loving in their doing of that, without showing off and without affectation. ﴿مِسْكِينًا﴾ (a needy person): he is the wanderer who is broken in asking. ﴿ويَتِيمًا﴾ (an orphan): he is the child who has no father. ﴿وأسِيرًا﴾ (a captive): the captive is well known, and he is from the disbelievers; this was said by Qatada. It is also said: he is from the Muslims who were left in the lands of the disbelievers as hostages and went out seeking ransom. Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is a captive from the people of the qibla. It is said: "wa-asiran" is a metaphor and a figure of speech. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: he is the imprisoned person. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: it is the wife. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: he is the slave and the prisoner. In a hadith: "Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive."

﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ﴾ (We feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance): this is by implying a saying (idmar al-qawl). It is permissible that they declared it explicitly, addressing those mentioned, to prevent them from reciprocating with the like or with thanks, since their kindness is done for the countenance of Allah the Exalted, so there is no sense in repaying the creation; and this is the apparent meaning. Mujahid said: As for them, they did not speak it, but Allah the Exalted knew it from them, so He praised them for it.

﴿لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً﴾ (We do not want from you any reward), that is, by deeds, ﴿ولا شُكُورًا﴾ (nor thanks), that is, praise by words. This verse was said to have been revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face. Al-Naqqash mentioned in this a very long narrative, apparently full of disagreement; in it there is an indication for the needy, the orphan and the captive, who are addressed with it in the house of prophethood, and an indication for Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, who addresses each of them; its outward form is disagreement, due to the baseness of its wording, the breaking of its verses and the triviality of its meanings.

﴿يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا﴾ (a stern day): attributing sternness to the day is a metaphor. Ibn 'Abbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from his eyes like tar. The majority read ﴿فَوَقاهُمُ﴾ (so Allah will protect them) with a light qaf; Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled.

﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً﴾ (and He will bestow upon them radiance), in place of the disbeliever's frown, ﴿وسُرُورًا﴾ (and joy): gladness in place of his grief; the radiance can only be with the joy of the soul and the coolness of the eye. The majority read ﴿وجَزاهُمْ﴾ (and will recompense them); 'Ali read "wa-jaza-hum" in the pattern of "fa'ala"... ﴿جَنَّةً وحَرِيرًا﴾ (a garden and silk): a garden in which is every pleasant food, and silk in which is a fine garment. The mention of silk with the garden is suitable, because they were preferred over hunger and nourishment.

﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها﴾ (they will see therein), that is, in Paradise, ﴿شَمْسًا﴾ (any sun), that is, the heat of the sun nor the severity of cold, meaning: there is no sun in it so that its heat would be seen and harm them, nor a zamharir (bitter cold) seen which would harm them with its severity; that is, its air is temperate. In a hadith: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj, neither hot nor cold." It is also said: they will not see in it a sun or a moon, and "al-zamharir" in the dialect of Tayy is the moon.

The majority read ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ (and near). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) coordinated with ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ (reclining). He also said: it is permissible that it be an attribute of the garden, so the meaning is: and He recompensed them with a near garden. Al-Zamakhshari said, in meaning, that it is a circumstantial state coordinated upon another state, which is "la yarawna" (they will not see), that is, not seeing; the waw entered to indicate that both matters are combined for them, as if it were said: and He recompensed them with a garden in which they combine between distance from heat and cold and the nearness of the shades over them. Abu Haywa read "wa-daniyatun" with raf', and al-Akhfash used it as evidence for the permissibility of raising the active participle without its being preceded by a dependent, such as your saying: "qa'imun al-zaydun" (standing are the Zaydun); but there is no proof in it, because the more apparent reading is that ﴿ظِلالُها﴾ (its shades) is the subject and ﴿ودانِيَةً﴾ is its predicate. Al-A'mash read "wa-daniyan 'alayhim," which is like His saying: ﴿خاشِعَةً أبْصارُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes humbled) [al-Ma'arij: 44]. Ubayy read "wa-danin" in the nominative, and with this al-Akhfash could be argued.

﴿وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها﴾ (and its clusters will be made low to be plucked). Qatada, Mujahid and Sufyan said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without effort; if he is sitting or reclining, it is likewise; this is its making easy, and neither distance nor thorn prevents the hand from it. As for the reading of the majority, "wa-daniyatan" in the accusative, "wa-dhullilat" is coordinated with "daniyatun," since it is in the sense of a singular, meaning: and made easy; and on the reading with raf', it is coordination of a verbal sentence upon a nominal sentence. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: and it has been made easy, "daniyatun" being raised or put in the accusative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verse 15–20 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that are [like] glass﴾ ﴿Glass of silver, which they have determined in measure﴾ ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾ ﴿A spring therein named Salsabil﴾ ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal. If you saw them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom﴾ ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them a pure drink﴾ [Al-Insan: 21] ﴿Indeed, this is a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [Al-Insan: 22] ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾ [Al-Insan: 23] ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord and do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [Al-Insan: 24] ﴿And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening﴾ [Al-Insan: 25] ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him and exalt Him through a long night﴾ [Al-Insan: 26] ﴿Indeed, these love the immediate and leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [Al-Insan: 27] ﴿We created them and strengthened their forms, and when We wish, We can replace them with their likes, with complete replacement﴾ [Al-Insan: 28] ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a path﴾ [Al-Insan: 29] ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan: 30] ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but the wrongdoers – He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Insan: 31]

When He, the Exalted, described their food, their dwelling and the manner of their sitting, He mentioned their drink, and He mentioned first the vessels from which they are given to drink. Ani (vessels) is the plural of inā' (vessel), and the explanation of akwab (cups) has already preceded. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read qawarira qawarira with tanwin in pause and in continuation, and substituting an alif in pause. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read both without tanwin (with the prohibition of diptote inflection). Ibn Kathir read the first with tanwin and the second without tanwin. Al-Zamakhshari said: This tanwin is a substitute for the alif of ițlaq (lengthening), because it is at the end of a verse (fasilah), and in the second it follows the first. End quote. He said likewise regarding the reading of those who read salasilā with tanwin: it is a substitute for the letter of ițlaq, treating the verse-endings as the lines of poetry, so just as tanwin enters the rhyming letters of the mutlaq (lengthened) type, signaling the abandonment of chanting, as the rajiz said:
Oh companion, what has stirred the tears to flow...
So this nun is a substitute for the alif, for if one were to chant, he would stop with the alif of ițlaq.

﴿min fiḍḍah﴾ means created from silver. The meaning of (kānat) is that He, the Exalted, brought them into being by His saying "Be, and it is" [Ya-Sin: 82], magnifying that wondrous creation which combines the whiteness and brightness of silver with the transparency and clarity of glass. Among this is His saying: ﴿a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾ [Al-Insan: 5]. Al-A'mash read qawarīru min fiḍḍatin with raf' (nominative), meaning: they are glasses. The majority read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ in the active voice, with the pronoun referring to the angels, or to those who circulate among them, or to the blessed ones; and the measure is according to the size of the hands, said by al-Rabi'. Or according to the measure of satisfaction, said by Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ is an attribute of qawārīra min fiḍḍah, and the meaning of their determining it is that they determined it in themselves in measures and shapes according to their desires, so it came as they determined it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those who circulate with them, indicated by His saying ﴿and they are circulated among them﴾, in that they determined its drink according to the measure of satisfaction, and this is the most delicious drink because it is according to the measure of their need, neither exceeding it nor falling short. From Mujahid: it neither overflows nor diminishes. End quote. Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Abza, Qatadah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Jahdari, ('Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Abu Haywah, 'Abbas (on the authority of Aban), al-Asma'i (on the authority of Abu 'Amr), and Ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq (on the authority of Ya'qub) read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ in the passive voice. Abu 'Ali said: It is as if the wording is "they determined over them," but in meaning there is an inversion, since the real meaning would be said: "it was determined for them." So it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, its keys would weigh down a band of strong men﴾ [Al-Qasas: 76], and like the saying of the Arabs: "When al-Jawza' rises, the stick strikes the lizard." Al-Zamakhshari said: Its direction is that it is from qadara, transferred from quddira, as you say: "I determined the thing" and "so-and-so made me determine it," if he made you able over it; its meaning: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine according to what they desired. End quote. Abu Hatim said: The vessels were determined according to the measure of their satisfaction. Some of the commentators explained this statement of Abu Hatim and said: there is an ellipsis upon an ellipsis, namely that it was determined according to the measure of their satisfaction in it, then omitted, so that the measure of their satisfaction became the object of the passive verb; then the verb was omitted, so their satisfaction stood in its place; then satisfaction was omitted, so the waw came in place of the ha' and mim when the noun before it was dropped, and the waw became the object of the passive verb, and the pronoun of the second object, in the sense of the verb's accusative, was joined to the verb after the waw which had changed from the ha' and mim, until it was made to stand in place of the subject. End quote. The closest explanation for this irregular reading is that the original is "qudd̲ara riyyuhum minhā taqdīran," the noun being dropped, namely "alladhī," and the pronoun was put in its place, so the sense became: "they were determined from it." Then the verb was extended, "min" was dropped, and the verb was connected to the pronoun directly, so it became "qaddarūhā." Thus there is nothing in it except the omission of a noun and an extension regarding the genitive.

The apparent meaning is that the cup is mixed with ginger, and the Arabs find it delightful and mention it in describing the saliva of women's mouths, as we have cited for them in the discussion of the vocabulary. Al-Zamakhshari said: the spring is named zanjabil because of the taste of ginger in it. End quote. Qatadah said: Zanjabil is the name of a spring in Paradise, from which those brought near drink pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise. Al-Kalbi said: it is given to drink from two cups: the first is mixed with camphor, and the second is mixed with ginger. ('Aynan) is a substitute for (ka's) by ellipsis, meaning: the cup of a spring; or a substitute for (zanjabil) according to Qatadah's view. It was also said: it is in the accusative by way of specification. The apparent meaning is that this spring is named Salsabil in the sense that it is described as being smooth in flow, easy in taste, and it should not be taken that salsabil is a proper name in reality, because if it were, it would be diptote due to femininity and definiteness. It has been narrated from Talhah that he read it without alif, making it a proper name for it. If it is a proper name, then the reading of the majority with tanwin fits the verse-endings, as some have said of (salasil) and (qawarir). What makes this acceptable is that it is a dialect of some Arabs, namely inflecting what most Arabs do not inflect. Al-Zamakhshari said: The letter ba' has been added in the structure until the word became quinqueliteral. End quote. He had mentioned: "sharāb salsal, salsāl, and salsīl." If he meant that it was actually added, then this is not sound, because the letter ba' is not among the letters of augmentation known in the science of grammar. If he meant that it is a letter that came within the root of the word, and it is not in salsīl nor in silsāl, then it is correct, and it would be among what agrees in meaning but differs in root.

Some grammarians said: Salsabil is a command to the Prophet ﷺ and his community to ask for the way to it. They attributed this statement to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and it must be discarded from books of tafsir. More astonishing than that is al-Zamakhshari's explanation of it and his occupation with relating it, while mentioning its attribution to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face and be pleased with him. Qatadah said: It is a spring that flows from beneath the Throne, from the Garden of Eden to the gardens. 'Ikrimah said: a spring whose water is smooth. Mujahid said: a spring whose flow is swift, smooth and easy to swallow. Muqatil said: a spring whose water flows continuously over them in their gatherings however they wish. The explanation of ﴿mukhalladūn﴾ has already preceded. The comparison of the young boys to scattered pearls is in their whiteness, the clarity of their colors, and their dispersal in the dwellings, serving the people of Paradise, coming and going. It was said: they are likened to fresh pearls when they are shaken out of their oyster shell, for that is more beautiful to the eye and more delightful to the soul.

The answer to (when you see) is ﴿bliss﴾, and the object of the conditional verb is omitted, being omitted for brevity, and the meaning is: "and when you cast your sight there." And "thamma" is an adverbial complement whose governing verb is "ra'ayta." It was said: the estimate is: "and when you see what is there," so "ma" was omitted, as it was omitted in His saying: ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [Al-An'am: 94], meaning: what is between you. Al-Zajjaj said, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: Whoever said its meaning is "ma thamma" has erred, because thamma is a complement of "ma," and it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave its complement. End quote. This is not an error agreed upon; rather the Kufans permitted it, and there are witnesses from the language of the Arabs, such as his saying:
Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises him and supports him, is equal.
That is: and whoever praises him, so he omitted the relative pronoun and left its complement. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "thamma" is an adverbial complement governed by (ra'ayta), or its meaning is an estimate: "you saw what is there," with "ma" omitted. End quote. This is corrupt, because if it is made an object of (ra'ayta), it cannot be a complement of "ma," since the governing element in that case would be an omitted verb, meaning: "what is settled there." The majority read "thamma" with a fatha on the tha'. Humayd al-A'raj read "thumma" with a damma on the tha', as a conjunction, and the answer to "idha" according to this is omitted, meaning: "and when you cast your sight, you will see bliss." As for the great kingdom, it was said: it is looking at Allah, the Exalted. Al-Suddi said: it is the angels asking permission to enter upon them. Most exegetes said: the great kingdom is the expansiveness of their places. Al-Kalbi said: great and wide; the least of them in rank in Paradise can see for a distance of a thousand years, seeing its farthest end as clearly as its nearest, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said this, and said: No one among the people of Paradise is without a thousand servant boys running to serve him, each of whom has a task different from that of his companions. Al-Tirmidhi, and I think he is al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, not Abu 'Isa the hafiz, author of al-Jami', said: it is the kingdom of creation and will, so that when He wills something, it is by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish﴾ [Qaf: 35]. It was said other than these sayings.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 15–20 (part 2 of 2):

Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, the people of Makkah and the majority of the Seven (al-sab'ah, the seven canonical Qur'an readers) recited ﴿ʿāliyahum﴾ [al-Insan: 21] with a fatha on the yā'. Ibn Abbas is also reported with a different reading from him. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Muhaysin, Nafi and Hamzah recited it with a sukun on the yā', and this is the transmission of Aban from Asim. Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Talhah and Zayd ibn Ali recited it with a ḍammah on the yā'. Also from al-A'mash and Aban, from Asim, is a fatha on the yā'. Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, al-Za'farani and also Aban recited ʿalayhim, with ʿalā as a preposition (ḥarf jarr). Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, recited ʿalathum with a feminine ta' (tā' al-ta'nīth) as a past-tense verb, so that thiyāb is the agent (fāʿil).

Whoever recited it with a ḍammah on the yā' takes it as a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is thiyāb. Whoever recited ʿalayhim with the preposition takes thiyāb as a subject. Whoever recited it with a fatha on the yā' and a sukun on the tā' takes it as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), which is a ḥāl from the pronoun attached to the object in ﴿yaṭūfu ʿalayhim﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]. The owner of the ḥāl is the ṭawf (going around) upon them, and the governing element (ʿāmil) is yaṭūfu.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "ʿāliyahum with the accusative is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿yaṭūfu ʿalayhim﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17] or in ﴿ḥasibtahum﴾, meaning: young boys will go around them, high (ʿāliyan) for those who are being served, wearing garments; or: you would think them scattered pearls, high for them, wearing garments. It is also possible that what is meant is: you see people of bliss and dominion, high upon them are garments." End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan comments: As for making it a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿ḥasibtahum﴾, this pronoun can only refer to the object, and here it refers to "young boys" (wildān). That is why he estimated ʿāliyahum as ʿāliyan lahum, meaning "for the young boys". This is not valid, because the pronouns that follow it show that they refer to those who are being served, from His words "and they are adorned" and "this was a reward for you" [al-Insan: 22]. Splitting the pronouns would make this one refer to one thing and that one to another, without any need or necessity, and that is not permitted.

As for making it a ḥāl from an omitted element, with the estimate "people of bliss", there is no need to claim an omission when the sentence is sound and eloquent without assuming that omitted element. Thiyāb is in the nominative, functioning as the agent of the ḥāl (marfū' 'alā al-fā'iliyyah bi-al-ḥāl).

Ibn Atiyyah said: "In the accusative reading, in both recitations, it may be a zarf (adverbial accusative), because it means 'above them'." End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan comments: ʿālin and ʿāliyah are active participles (ism al-fā'il). To establish that they function as adverbial accusatives, one needs a report from the Arabs that says ʿāliyaka or ʿāliyatuka thawb (a garment is above you). The majority recited thiyābu without tanwīn, as an idāfah (construct) to Sundus. Ibn Abla and Abu Haywah recited ʿalayhim thiyābun sundusun khuḍrun wa-istabraqun, with all three in the nominative. Sundus is nominative as an adjective, since it is a noun of genus (ism jins), as you say thawbun ḥarīrun, meaning "a garment of silk". Khuḍr is nominative as an adjective too, because green is a color. Istabraq is nominative by coordination with it. It is an adjective placed in the position of the noun described; the estimate is wa-thiyābun istabraqun, meaning "garments of brocade", that is, of brocade.

Al-Hasan, Isa, Nafi and Hafs recited khuḍrun with nominative on both. Al-Arabiyyan (the two grammarians, namely the Kufan and Basran readings of the Seven, i.e. Ibn Amir/Ibn Kathir school as commonly identified in this context) and Nafi in one transmission recited ﴿khuḍrun﴾ [al-Insan: 21] in the nominative as an adjective of thiyāb, and ﴿istabraqin﴾ [al-Rahman: 54] in the genitive by coordination with sundus. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr recited khuḍrin in the genitive as an adjective of sundus, and istabraqun in the nominative by coordination with "thiyāb". Al-A'mash, Talhah, al-Hasan and Abu Amr (with variants transmitted from two of them) recited... Hamzah and al-Kisa'i: the description of a noun of genus (ism al-jins), between which and its singular there is a tā' of feminization, is permissible, and the plural is eloquent, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], and He said: ﴿and the tall palm trees﴾ [Qaf: 10], making the ḥāl plural. If they pluralized the description of a noun of genus that has no tā' of feminization between it and its singular, when it is preceded by al-, as in their saying: "The gold dinar, yellow, and the silver dirham, white, destroyed the people", where pluralizing the description of both is not sound. Rather, it is permissible, and the grammarians cited it as permissible without being ugly.

Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-istabraqun﴾ [al-Insan: 21], and this has already been discussed, with the discussion about it in al-Kahf. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Here it was recited wa-istabraqan, in the accusative in a position of genitive, as diptote (mamnū' min al-ṣarf) because it is a loanword (a'jamī)." This is an error, because it is a noun (nakirah) that can take the definite article: you say al-istabraq. Unless Ibn Muhaysin claims that it has become a proper name for this type of garment. It was also recited wa-istabraqa with a connecting hamzah (hamzat al-waṣl) and a fatha, as if it were named after the form istaf'ala from al-bariq (glitter). This is also not correct, because it is a well-known loanword whose Arabicization is established, and its original form is istabrah." End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan comments: His words "unless Ibn Muhaysin claims", and his words later "it was recited wa-istabraqa with a connecting alif and a fatha", show that Ibn Muhaysin's recitation is with a cut hamzah (hamzat al-qaṭ') and a fatha on the qāf. What is transmitted from him in the books of recitations is that he recited with a connecting alif and a fatha on the qāf. Abu Hatim said: "It is not permissible. The correct view is that it is a noun of genus that should not bear a pronoun; this is supported by the entry of the definite article (lām al-ma'rifah) on it. The correct reading is with a cut hamzah, conforming to the recitation of the community." End of quotation.

I say: Ibn Muhaysin is an eminent and well-known reciter, known for knowledge of Arabic, and he took from great scholars. His recitation requires a justification, and it is this: he makes istaf'ala from al-bariq. One says bariqa and istabraqa, like ʿajiba and istaʿjaba (to be amazed).

Since His words ﴿khuḍrun﴾ [al-Insan: 21] indicate greenness, which is the color of that sundus, and greenness, because of its intensity, may involve darkness and dimness, He informed us that in that color there is a gleam and beauty that removes its dimness. So istabraqa is a past-tense verb, and its pronoun refers either to sundus or to the greenness indicated by His words ﴿khuḍrun﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. This analysis is better than condemning one who knows Arabic, and than mistaking a trustworthy authority, namely ﴿silver bracelets﴾ [al-Insan: 21]; and in another place "of gold". That is, they are adorned with both of them alternately, or both together, as happens to women in this world.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "How beautiful it is for the wrist to have two bracelets, one of gold and one of silver." End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan comments: His words "bil-mi'ṣam" (on the wrist) may be the object of aḥsana (how beautiful), or a substitute (badal) for it, or the object of aḥsana, and it has been separated from it by a prepositional phrase. If it is the first, it is not permissible, because it is not established that the preposition bā' is added to the object of the comparative exclamation form af'ala (for exclamation). You do not say "How beautiful by Zayd", meaning "how beautiful Zayd is". If it is the second, there is disagreement about this type of separation, and what is transmitted from Sibawayh is that it is not permissible. A Muwallad (a later, non-classical Arabic speaker) among us, when speaking, should be careful in his speech to avoid what is disputed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verse 15–20 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that are [like] glass﴾ ﴿Glass of silver, which they have determined in measure﴾ ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾ ﴿A spring therein named Salsabil﴾ ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal. If you saw them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom﴾ ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them a pure drink﴾ [Al-Insan: 21] ﴿Indeed, this is a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [Al-Insan: 22] ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾ [Al-Insan: 23] ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord and do not obey from among them a sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [Al-Insan: 24] ﴿And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening﴾ [Al-Insan: 25] ﴿And during the night prostrate to Him and exalt Him through a long night﴾ [Al-Insan: 26] ﴿Indeed, these love the immediate and leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [Al-Insan: 27] ﴿We created them and strengthened their forms, and when We wish, We can replace them with their likes, with complete replacement﴾ [Al-Insan: 28] ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a path﴾ [Al-Insan: 29] ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan: 30] ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but the wrongdoers – He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Insan: 31]

When He, the Exalted, described their food, their dwelling and the manner of their sitting, He mentioned their drink, and He mentioned first the vessels from which they are given to drink. Ani (vessels) is the plural of inā' (vessel), and the explanation of akwab (cups) has already preceded. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read qawarira qawarira with tanwin in pause and in continuation, and substituting an alif in pause. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read both without tanwin (with the prohibition of diptote inflection). Ibn Kathir read the first with tanwin and the second without tanwin. Al-Zamakhshari said: This tanwin is a substitute for the alif of ițlaq (lengthening), because it is at the end of a verse (fasilah), and in the second it follows the first. End quote. He said likewise regarding the reading of those who read salasilā with tanwin: it is a substitute for the letter of ițlaq, treating the verse-endings as the lines of poetry, so just as tanwin enters the rhyming letters of the mutlaq (lengthened) type, signaling the abandonment of chanting, as the rajiz said:
Oh companion, what has stirred the tears to flow...
So this nun is a substitute for the alif, for if one were to chant, he would stop with the alif of ițlaq.

﴿min fiḍḍah﴾ means created from silver. The meaning of (kānat) is that He, the Exalted, brought them into being by His saying "Be, and it is" [Ya-Sin: 82], magnifying that wondrous creation which combines the whiteness and brightness of silver with the transparency and clarity of glass. Among this is His saying: ﴿a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾ [Al-Insan: 5]. Al-A'mash read qawarīru min fiḍḍatin with raf' (nominative), meaning: they are glasses. The majority read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ in the active voice, with the pronoun referring to the angels, or to those who circulate among them, or to the blessed ones; and the measure is according to the size of the hands, said by al-Rabi'. Or according to the measure of satisfaction, said by Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ is an attribute of qawārīra min fiḍḍah, and the meaning of their determining it is that they determined it in themselves in measures and shapes according to their desires, so it came as they determined it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those who circulate with them, indicated by His saying ﴿and they are circulated among them﴾, in that they determined its drink according to the measure of satisfaction, and this is the most delicious drink because it is according to the measure of their need, neither exceeding it nor falling short. From Mujahid: it neither overflows nor diminishes. End quote. Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Abza, Qatadah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Jahdari, ('Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Abu Haywah, 'Abbas (on the authority of Aban), al-Asma'i (on the authority of Abu 'Amr), and Ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq (on the authority of Ya'qub) read ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ in the passive voice. Abu 'Ali said: It is as if the wording is "they determined over them," but in meaning there is an inversion, since the real meaning would be said: "it was determined for them." So it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, its keys would weigh down a band of strong men﴾ [Al-Qasas: 76], and like the saying of the Arabs: "When al-Jawza' rises, the stick strikes the lizard." Al-Zamakhshari said: Its direction is that it is from qadara, transferred from quddira, as you say: "I determined the thing" and "so-and-so made me determine it," if he made you able over it; its meaning: they were made able over it as they wished, and it was permitted to them to determine according to what they desired. End quote. Abu Hatim said: The vessels were determined according to the measure of their satisfaction. Some of the commentators explained this statement of Abu Hatim and said: there is an ellipsis upon an ellipsis, namely that it was determined according to the measure of their satisfaction in it, then omitted, so that the measure of their satisfaction became the object of the passive verb; then the verb was omitted, so their satisfaction stood in its place; then satisfaction was omitted, so the waw came in place of the ha' and mim when the noun before it was dropped, and the waw became the object of the passive verb, and the pronoun of the second object, in the sense of the verb's accusative, was joined to the verb after the waw which had changed from the ha' and mim, until it was made to stand in place of the subject. End quote. The closest explanation for this irregular reading is that the original is "qudd̲ara riyyuhum minhā taqdīran," the noun being dropped, namely "alladhī," and the pronoun was put in its place, so the sense became: "they were determined from it." Then the verb was extended, "min" was dropped, and the verb was connected to the pronoun directly, so it became "qaddarūhā." Thus there is nothing in it except the omission of a noun and an extension regarding the genitive.

The apparent meaning is that the cup is mixed with ginger, and the Arabs find it delightful and mention it in describing the saliva of women's mouths, as we have cited for them in the discussion of the vocabulary. Al-Zamakhshari said: the spring is named zanjabil because of the taste of ginger in it. End quote. Qatadah said: Zanjabil is the name of a spring in Paradise, from which those brought near drink pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise. Al-Kalbi said: it is given to drink from two cups: the first is mixed with camphor, and the second is mixed with ginger. ('Aynan) is a substitute for (ka's) by ellipsis, meaning: the cup of a spring; or a substitute for (zanjabil) according to Qatadah's view. It was also said: it is in the accusative by way of specification. The apparent meaning is that this spring is named Salsabil in the sense that it is described as being smooth in flow, easy in taste, and it should not be taken that salsabil is a proper name in reality, because if it were, it would be diptote due to femininity and definiteness. It has been narrated from Talhah that he read it without alif, making it a proper name for it. If it is a proper name, then the reading of the majority with tanwin fits the verse-endings, as some have said of (salasil) and (qawarir). What makes this acceptable is that it is a dialect of some Arabs, namely inflecting what most Arabs do not inflect. Al-Zamakhshari said: The letter ba' has been added in the structure until the word became quinqueliteral. End quote. He had mentioned: "sharāb salsal, salsāl, and salsīl." If he meant that it was actually added, then this is not sound, because the letter ba' is not among the letters of augmentation known in the science of grammar. If he meant that it is a letter that came within the root of the word, and it is not in salsīl nor in silsāl, then it is correct, and it would be among what agrees in meaning but differs in root.

Some grammarians said: Salsabil is a command to the Prophet ﷺ and his community to ask for the way to it. They attributed this statement to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and it must be discarded from books of tafsir. More astonishing than that is al-Zamakhshari's explanation of it and his occupation with relating it, while mentioning its attribution to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face and be pleased with him. Qatadah said: It is a spring that flows from beneath the Throne, from the Garden of Eden to the gardens. 'Ikrimah said: a spring whose water is smooth. Mujahid said: a spring whose flow is swift, smooth and easy to swallow. Muqatil said: a spring whose water flows continuously over them in their gatherings however they wish. The explanation of ﴿mukhalladūn﴾ has already preceded. The comparison of the young boys to scattered pearls is in their whiteness, the clarity of their colors, and their dispersal in the dwellings, serving the people of Paradise, coming and going. It was said: they are likened to fresh pearls when they are shaken out of their oyster shell, for that is more beautiful to the eye and more delightful to the soul.

And "thamma" is an adverbial complement whose governing verb is "ra'ayta." It was said: the estimate is: "and when you see what is there," so "ma" was omitted, as it was omitted in His saying: ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [Al-An'am: 94], meaning: what is between you. Al-Zajjaj said, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, saying: Whoever said its meaning is "ma thamma" has erred, because thamma is a complement of "ma," and it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave its complement. End quote. This is not an error agreed upon; rather the Kufans permitted it, and there are witnesses from the language of the Arabs, such as his saying:
Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises him and supports him, is equal.
That is: and whoever praises him, so he omitted the relative pronoun and left its complement. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "thamma" is an adverbial complement governed by (ra'ayta), or its meaning is an estimate: "you saw what is there," with "ma" omitted. End quote. This is corrupt, because if it is made an object of (ra'ayta), it cannot be a complement of "ma," since the governing element in that case would be an omitted verb, meaning: "what is settled there." The majority read "thamma" with a fatha on the tha'. Humayd al-A'raj read "thumma" with a damma on the tha', as a conjunction, and the answer to "idha" according to this is omitted, meaning: "and when you cast your sight, you will see bliss." As for the great kingdom, it was said: it is looking at Allah, the Exalted. Al-Suddi said: it is the angels asking permission to enter upon them. Most exegetes said: the great kingdom is the expansiveness of their places. Al-Kalbi said: great and wide; the least of them in rank in Paradise can see for a distance of a thousand years, seeing its farthest end as clearly as its nearest, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said this, and said: No one among the people of Paradise is without a thousand servant boys running to serve him, each of whom has a task different from that of his companions.
