Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the position of *an yasha'a Allah* (that God wills)? I say: it is in the accusative as an adverbial of time. Its original form is: 'except at the time of God's will.' Likewise Ibn Mas'ud read: *illa ma yasha'u Allah*, because *ma* with the verb is like the verb with it." End of quote. They (the grammarians) stated that nothing can take the place of the adverb of time except an explicitly stated verbal noun, as when you say: "I will come to you at the crowing of the rooster," but they do not permit: "I will come to you that the rooster crows," nor "what the rooster crows." Based on this, what al-Zamakhshari said is not permissible.

﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾: they are the believers. The majority read *wa-l-zalimin* (and the wrongdoers) in the accusative, with an implied verb explained by His saying: ﴿He has prepared for them﴾. Its estimate is: "and He punishes the wrongdoers." This is from the category of *ishtighal* (the object-preceding construction, where the noun is governed by a verb supplied to match a following verb). Ibn al-Zubayr, Aban ibn 'Uthman and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *wa-l-zalimun* (and the wrongdoers) in the nominative, conjoining a nominal clause to a verbal clause, which is permissible and good. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *wa-li-l-zalimin* (and for the wrongdoers) with the preposition *li* (for), which is connected with *a'adda lahum* as an emphasis. It is not permissible for it to be from the category of *ishtighal*, with a verb estimated to be explained by the verb that follows, so that the estimate would be: "and He prepared for the wrongdoers, He prepared for them." This is the position of the majority, and there is a weak disagreement about it mentioned in grammar. You say: *bi-Zayd marrartu bihi* (as for Zayd, I passed by him), and the estimate would be: "I passed by Zayd, I passed by him," and it would be from the category of *ishtighal*. But what is known and transmitted from the Arabs is the accusative of the noun and the explanation of *marartu* (I passed) by the later verb, and whatever resembles it in meaning as a past verb.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 76, verses 21–31:**

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾. *Tahur* (pure) is an intensive adjective (*sifa mubalagha*) meaning extremely pure. It derives from an intransitive verb (*fi'l lazim*). Its purity lies in the fact that they are not commanded to avoid it, unlike the wine of this world, which is in the Law an abomination (*rijs*). Or its purity lies in the fact that it has not been trodden on by dirty feet, touched by a filthy hand, or placed in a vessel that was not cleaned. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) mentioned this more fully and then said: "Or because it does not turn into impurity, since it exudes from their bodies a sweat that has a scent like musk." End of quote. This last view was held by Abu Qilaba, al-Nakha'i and Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said: "It does not turn into urine, but becomes a sweat from the bodies more pleasant than musk."

﴿Indeed, this﴾: that is, the everlasting bliss. ﴿was for you a reward﴾: that is, for your good deeds. ﴿and your striving was appreciated﴾: that is, accepted and rewarded. Qatada said: "God has appreciated little striving." This is understood as an implied speech, meaning: "It will be said to them." This saying addressed to them is a way of congratulating and gladdening them, the opposite of what is said to the one being punished: "This is for your evil deed," which increases his grief and sorrow.

When He first mentioned the state of man and divided people into the disobedient and the obedient, He mentioned what He honoured His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with. He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Qur'an to you﴾, and commanded him to be patient with His command. The emphasis with *inna* corresponds to the content of the statement and the meaning of the one spoken of. The verb is also emphasised with a verbal noun (*masdar*).

﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or ingrate﴾. Qatada said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who said: 'If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely step on his neck.' So God revealed: ﴿And do not obey﴾," and the rest of the verse. The prohibition against obeying each one of them separately is stronger than the prohibition against obeying them together, because it entails a prohibition against obeying either one, since obeying both includes obeying one of them. If one said, "Do not strike Zayd and 'Amr," it could be understood as a prohibition against striking both of them together, not against striking either one of them. Abu 'Ubayda said: *aw* (or) here has the meaning of *wa* (and). The ingrate, although he is also a sinner, is described with added emphasis on disbelief. Since the description of "ingrate" is distinct from "sinner" merely as sin, the distinction is valid and the conjunction is appropriate.

It has been said: the sinner is 'Utba, and the ingrate is al-Walid, because 'Utba used to ride upon sins and indulge in all kinds of wickedness, while al-Walid was extreme in disbelief and fierce in obstinacy.

﴿And remember the name of your Lord at dawn﴾: meaning the dawn prayer. ((And in the evening)): the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And during the night﴾: the sunset and night prayers. Ibn Zayd and others said: that was obligatory and was abrogated (*nasakh*), so there is no obligation except the five prayers. Others said: it is definitive (*muhkam*) in the sense of recommendation.

﴿Indeed, these﴾: a reference to the disbelievers. ﴿love the immediate﴾: they prefer it over the Hereafter. ﴿and leave behind them﴾: that is, before them, which is the time they will face. ﴿a heavy day﴾: the heaviness is attributed to the day metaphorically for its intensity and terror, from the heaviness of a burden that wearies its bearer. The explanation of *al-asr* (binding) was mentioned in the surah of Muhammad (al-Qital).

﴿And when We will﴾: that is, to replace them by destroying them. ﴿We will replace their likes﴾ with those who obey. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its proper form should be with *in* (if) not *idha* (when), as in His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾ [Muhammad 38], and ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾ [al-Nisa 133]." End of quote. He means that they said: *idha* is used for what is certain, and *in* for what is possible, and He, exalted is He, did not will. However, *idha* may be placed in the position of *in*, and *in* in the position of *idha*, as in His saying: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ [al-Anbiya 34].

﴿Indeed, this﴾: that is, the surah, or the verses of the Qur'an, or the whole of the Law. It is not a matter of choice, but of warning against taking any path other than the path of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is for whoever wills among those who choose good for themselves and the final outcome. Taking a path to God is an expression of drawing near to Him and seeking a means to Him through obedience." ﴿And you do not will﴾: obedience. ﴿except that God wills﴾, compelling them to it. ﴿Indeed, God is ever Knowing﴾ of their states and what will come from them, ((Wise)): in that He created them while knowing them.

End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazili subtlety (*dasisat al-i'tizal*). The two Arab readers (al-'Arabiyyan) and Ibn Kathir read *wa-ma yashau'na* with the third-person (ya of absence). The rest of the seven readers (al-Sab'a) read it with the second-person (ta of address).
